source: Kahneman (2003) Maps of bounded rationality (Nobel lecture, Am Psychol)
finding: Defines System 1 as fast, automatic, effortless, associative, hard to control; System 2 as slower, serial, effortful, rule-governed. System 2 monitors System 1 but the monitoring is lax, so many intuitive answers go out unchecked.
numbers: Bat-and-ball item (Frederick, personal communication): 50% (47/93) of Princeton students and 56% (164/293) of Michigan students answered 10 cents.
quote: the monitoring is normally quite lax, and allows many intuitive judgments to be expressed, including some that are erroneous
limits: Lecture summary, not the original data paper. Monitoring is a stated assumption, not directly measured here.
agent_relevance: Default-interventionist core claim: the first answer ships unless a check fires. Our agent must make checks code-triggered, since a model's own monitoring is also lax.

source: Kahneman (2003) Maps of bounded rationality (Nobel lecture)
finding: Attribute substitution: a hard question (probability) is answered by an easy accessible one (similarity). In the Linda problem, rankings by probability and by representativeness correlate .99. Conjunction errors are strong between-subjects and weaker in direct within-subject comparison.
numbers: Linda: 85% ranked the conjunction above the single item when ranking by representativeness, 89% when ranking by probability (mean-rank correlation .99).
limits: Statistically trained graduate students still used representativeness by default; training helped only in the stripped-down version, where errors dropped sharply. Within-subject direct comparison reduces errors.
agent_relevance: Shows what training does: it adds rules usable under cues, it does not remove the fast heuristic. Same for prompts: warnings alone do not remove the fast path.

source: Kahneman (2003) Maps of bounded rationality (Nobel lecture)
finding: Conditions that weaken System 2: time pressure, concurrent cognitive load, off-peak time of day, good mood. Conditions that help it: higher intelligence, need for cognition, exposure to statistical thinking.
numbers: Cites Finucane 2000 (time pressure), Gilbert 1989/1991 (load), Bodenhausen 1990 (circadian), Stanovich and West 2002 (intelligence). No effect sizes given.
limits: Review citations, not new experiments.
agent_relevance: Maps to budget and load: under token or context pressure the agent will drift to its fast path; S0 should reserve budget for hard items.

source: Pelaccia, Tardif, Triby, Charlin (2011) An analysis of clinical reasoning through the dual-process theory (Med Educ Online)
finding: Maps dual-process onto medicine: pattern recognition = intuitive system, hypothetico-deduction = analytic system. Reasoning starts intuitively; the analytic system then confirms or rejects. Both are used by novices and experts. Analytic control is more likely when time permits, stakes are high, the case is complex or ill-defined.
numbers: Neufeld et al. as reported: a correct hypothesis in the first 5 minutes gives about 95% chance of the right final diagnosis. Cites experiments where pure analytic or pure non-analytic instructions did worse than a combination.
limits: Narrative review, 2011. Text itself admits it is unclear whether physicians really work within the dual-process frame. Gives no new data.
agent_relevance: Supports S0 default: generate fast, then verify. The switch rule is unclear in the field, so our switch must be an explicit code rule.

source: Pelaccia et al. (2011) An analysis of clinical reasoning through the dual-process theory
finding: Errors cannot be pinned on one system: a wrong intuitive answer may come from poor intuition or from a failed analytic monitor; a wrong analytic answer may come from a failed analytic step or from intuition that offered no good early hypothesis. Analytic answers are not shown to be better than intuitive ones; both are error-prone (Norman and Eva).
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Hogarth: kind versus wicked learning environments decide whether intuition can be trusted.
limits: Secondary source. Reliability of intuition is called a sticking point in the field.
agent_relevance: Warns against 'trust slow thinking'. Trust should depend on whether a checkable signal exists, not on the mode label.

source: Tay, Ryan, Ryan (2016) Systems 1 and 2 thinking processes and cognitive reflection testing in medical students (Can Med Educ J)
finding: Cognitive Reflection Test given to medical students. About 10% gave the intuitive answer to all three items and 44% got all three right. Intuitive share fell and correct share rose from item 1 to item 3.
numbers: N=128 (years 2-4 of a 5-year degree). 13/128 (10%) all intuitive; 44% all correct; only 3-13% gave answers that were neither. Non-native English speakers (n=11) scored lower: mean 1.0 vs 2.12 correct (p<.01).
limits: Single school, cross-sectional, no link to clinical performance (authors say so). Small non-native subgroup.
agent_relevance: Even selected, trained people fall for the first-impression trap about half the time on simple items; the trap is suppression, not knowledge.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (arXiv 2206.14576; PNAS 2023)
finding: GPT-3 was given the three Cognitive Reflection Test items and gave the intuitive wrong answer on all three. On 12 classic vignettes (Linda, hospital sizes, Wason, cab problem and others) it answered 6 correctly and all 12 in a human-like way (correct or a known human error).
numbers: CRT: 3/3 items intuitive-wrong. Vignettes: 6/12 correct, 12/12 human-like. A cab-problem variant got an answer that was neither correct nor human-like.
limits: Single model, one run per item, no chain-of-thought, few items. Read the arXiv v1; the published version may differ.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that a plain LLM's first-token path behaves like System 1. Baseline for judging any scaffold that adds a slow step.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT (arXiv 2212.05206; Nat Comput Sci)
finding: Bespoke CRT and semantic-illusion tasks (200 total) run across GPT-3 sizes, ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4. Older GPT-3 fell for intuitive traps more than humans; ChatGPT-4 almost never did. Task difficulty matched human studies.
numbers: CRT correct: humans 38% (original study 41%, n=3,428); GPT-3-davinci-003 5%; ChatGPT-3.5 59%; ChatGPT-4 96%. Intuitive-wrong: davinci-003 80%, humans 55%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, ChatGPT-4 0%. Semantic illusions: davinci-003 fell for them 72% of the time; correct 18% davinci-003, 74% ChatGPT-3.5, 88% ChatGPT-4.
limits: Tasks are known-trap puzzles, likely in training data; newer models may have memorised them. Not medical.
agent_relevance: The fast/slow gap shrinks with model capability, so a mode switch tuned on a weak model may be wasted on a strong one. Re-measure per model.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) arXiv 2212.05206
finding: Chain-of-thought acts like a System 2 switch for weak models: forcing step-by-step raised correct answers on davinci-003. Removing it from strong models barely hurt them, so their skill is internalised.
numbers: davinci-003 with CoT: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive-wrong 80% to 29%. Blocking CoT: ChatGPT-3.5 correct unchanged (change 4%, p=.49); ChatGPT-4 correct 95% to 88% and intuitive 0% to 10%. CoT share of ChatGPT responses fell 97% to 0% (3.5) and 84% to 0% (4).
limits: Small item set; CoT-block done by prompt instruction.
agent_relevance: A strong model may not need a forced slow step on trap puzzles; forcing one on easy items only costs tokens (G7).

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) arXiv 2212.05206
finding: Few-shot examples teach a weak model to avoid the traps; it learns an intuition for the trick rather than a slow routine.
numbers: Reported gains of 2% to 92% accuracy after two examples on one task type, 12% to 92% after seven on another, and about 0% to 78% after 30 examples on a harder type.
limits: Which task maps to which number was not fully checked in the extracted text; use the ranges only.
agent_relevance: Matches the dual-process view that trained System 1 can replace System 2 on a known trap class; supports caching known-trap cases as retrieved rules.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too) (arXiv 2311.11829)
finding: S2A has the model first rewrite the prompt to strip irrelevant or opinionated text, then answer from the rewrite. This removes a System-1 style sycophancy effect.
numbers: Factual QA with opinions in the prompt (LLaMA-2-70B-chat): baseline 62.8%, oracle unopinionated prompt 82.0%, S2A 80.3%. GSM-IC with irrelevant sentences: 51.7% to 61.3%. Longform arguments: objectivity up 57.4%.
limits: Extra generation pass; one base model family; gains tied to prompts with planted distractors.
agent_relevance: A concrete operator: restate the problem without distractors before solving. Fits our restate slot as a code-ordered step, not a doubt step.

source: Yu, Xu, Weston (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1 (arXiv 2407.06023)
finding: Self-supervised distillation turns slow multi-step prompting outputs into direct answers. It works for rephrase-and-respond, System 2 Attention and Branch-Solve-Merge, but fails for chain-of-thought math.
numbers: Last-letter task (Llama-2-70B-chat): base 30.0%, 2-step RaR 39.5%, 1-step RaR 44.5%, distilled 2-step RaR 98.0%. Coin flip: base 56.1%, distilled 75.69%. TriviaQA with bias: S2A 76.0%, distilled 81.3% with far fewer tokens. GSM8k: System 1 9.40%, CoT/System 2 52.77%, distilled System 2 only 7.13%.
limits: Distillation needs a self-consistency filter (ablation without it lost accuracy). Tables were read from a two-column PDF extract, so column mapping is partly inferred.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: some tasks cannot move to the fast path; multi-step arithmetic-like work needs the slow trace. S0 must know task class before choosing mode.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: a generative agent with fast and slow thinking for complex interactive tasks (arXiv 2305.17390, NeurIPS 2023)
finding: Explicit dual-process agent: a small fine-tuned Swift module acts by default; a GPT-4 Sage module plans only when triggered. Four code-checked switch rules: stuck (5 steps with zero reward), invalid action, critical decision, unexpected observation.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 task types: SwiftSage 84.7 vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3. Tokens per action: SwiftSage 757 vs SayCan 1,856, ReAct 1,971, Reflexion 2,983. With GPT-3.5: ReAct 36.43 to 19.76, SwiftSage 62.22.
limits: Swift is trained by imitation on the same benchmark; text game, not diagnosis; main runs use GPT-4. Switch rules are hand-built heuristics.
agent_relevance: Closest working template for S0: fast default, slow on code-detected signals (stuck, invalid, critical). Matches G1. Not a medical test.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2024/2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse (arXiv 2410.21333)
finding: Takes six tasks where verbal deliberation hurts humans and tests CoT on frontier models. In three tasks CoT hurt models strongly; in the others effects were mixed. Human deliberation harm is a usable heuristic for where slow thinking backfires.
numbers: Artificial grammar learning: GPT-4o 87.5% zero-shot vs 64.4% CoT (-23.1 points); o1-preview vs GPT-4o on a subset: 57.7% vs 94.0% (-36.3). Face recognition: GPT-4o 64.0% to 51.2%, Claude 3 Opus 44.0% to 29.6%. Data with exceptions: models needed up to 331% more rounds to learn labels with CoT. Tree of Thoughts on grammar task 64.55%, still far below 94.00% zero-shot.
limits: Human parallel is imperfect; Claude 3.5 Sonnet showed small or no drop on some tasks (grammar -1.8, p=.969); three of six tasks showed mixed or no harm.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence against 'slow is always better'. S0 should not force deliberation on pattern or similarity tasks; supports a measured per-task-type mode choice.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models (npj Digit Med)
finding: BiasMedQA: 1,273 USMLE questions each with one of seven bias sentences naming a wrong answer. All six models lost accuracy. Three prompt mitigations (bias education, one-shot, few-shot) improved but did not restore accuracy.
numbers: Unbiased accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama-13B 33.4%. Average drop with bias: GPT-4 -5.1%, Mixtral -7.7%, GPT-3.5 -17.8%, Llama-2-70B -20.1%. Worst bias false-consensus (-24.9% average); confirmation least (-8.1%). Education prompt +3.5 to +6.5 points; GPT-4 few-shot average 75.2%.
limits: Biases are planted by one sentence, not natural; multiple choice; warning prompt gave only small gains and worsened some cultural-bias cases.
agent_relevance: An LLM takes the planted wrong anchor like a System 1 answer. Warnings help a little; the code layer should strip social and prior-answer cues from the input.

source: Norman, Monteiro, Sherbino, Ilgen, Schmidt, Mamede (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking (Acad Med)
finding: Abstract read only (Europe PMC). Errors come from both Type 1 and Type 2; Type 1 errors from associative memory, Type 2 errors from limited working memory. Bias teaching does not reduce errors; knowledge reorganisation gives small but consistent gains.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
quote: Educational strategies directed at the recognition of biases are ineffective in reducing errors
limits: Abstract only. Link is a search link because the exact record id was not verified.
agent_relevance: Key warning for S0: 'think slower' is not a fix; add knowledge or checks.

source: Mamede, van Gog, van den Berge, et al. (2010) Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents (JAMA)
finding: Abstract read via Europe PMC. Second-year residents using non-analytic reasoning made availability-bias errors after seeing similar prior cases; structured reflection raised accuracy.
numbers: N=36 (18 first-year, 18 second-year). Second-years scored 1.55 on cases similar to prior ones vs 2.19 on others (P=.03). Reflection scores on similar cases: 2.03 (second-year), 2.31 (first-year), P=.006. Scale maximum 4.0.
limits: Small N, written cases, one centre. Reflection was structured re-analysis, not 'slow down'. First-years showed the opposite direction in the bias pattern (P=.046).
agent_relevance: Structured re-analysis from the case findings helped; supports a slow step that re-derives from data, not a mood of caution.

source: Ilgen, Bowen, McIntyre, et al. (2013) Comparing diagnostic performance under testing conditions that encourage automatic or analytic thought (Acad Med)
finding: Abstract only. Instructing clinicians to give a first impression vs follow a directed systematic search gave no accuracy difference.
numbers: N=393 clinicians (students, trainees, faculty), multicentre randomised, 2011-2012. Instruction effect F(1,379)=2.44, P=.12. Complexity F=965.2, experience F=39.6, both P<.001. First-impression scores correlated better with USMLE.
limits: Abstract only; vignettes not live patients.
agent_relevance: Mode instruction alone barely moves accuracy; difficulty and knowledge dominate. Do not expect large gains from a mode label.

source: Sherbino, Yip, Dore, Siu, Norman (2011) The effectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to decrease diagnostic error (Teach Learn Med)
finding: Abstract only. Exploratory cognitive forcing training for senior students; application and retention were poor.
numbers: N=56 emergency-medicine students; 47 tested immediately, 9 after 2 weeks; 6 test cases.
limits: Exploratory; the later controlled trial (Sherbino 2014) is listed as 'ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies' but was not read.
agent_relevance: Taught slow-down procedures transfer poorly in humans; for an agent the equivalent is a coded check, not an instruction.

source: Croskerry (2009) A universal model of diagnostic reasoning (Acad Med)
finding: Abstract only. Proposes the dual-process model for medicine: System 1 (heuristic, intuitive) and System 2 (systematic, analytical). Author cautions that not all reasoning fits neatly in one system.
numbers: None in abstract.
limits: Abstract read; the full model figure (recognition, override routes, calibration) is background knowledge, not verified here.
agent_relevance: Source of the default-interventionist template S0 inherits; the criticism is that mode labels are too coarse.

source: Monteiro, Sherbino, Sibbald, Norman (2020) Critical thinking, biases and dual processing: the enduring myth of generalisable skills (Med Educ)
finding: Abstract only. Argues thinking-skill and bias-awareness curricula lack evidence; knowledge breadth and depth drive expert performance.
numbers: None in abstract.
limits: Critical review by authors who also wrote the 2017 review; an advocacy position.
agent_relevance: Supports putting effort into retrieved knowledge and checks, not general 'be careful' prompts.

source: Evans and Stanovich (2013) Dual-process theories of higher cognition: advancing the debate (Perspect Psychol Sci)
finding: Not opened (publisher blocked). From background knowledge only: replaces System 1/2 with Type 1 (autonomous, no working memory needed) and Type 2 (needs working memory, hypothetical thinking) and answers five criticisms. Defining features, not correlated features such as speed, must separate the types.
numbers: None.
limits: Background knowledge only; verify wording before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Define our types by function (needs a written intermediate trace or not), not by speed.

source: Frederick (2005) Cognitive reflection and decision making (J Econ Perspect)
finding: Not opened (publisher blocked). Three-item CRT; the bat-and-ball answer 10 cents is the intuitive trap. The 41% correct, n=3,428 figure was cross-checked via Hagendorff et al. (opened).
numbers: Only the 41% / n=3,428 figure is cross-checked here.
limits: Mostly unverified.
agent_relevance: CRT-style items are the standard probe for an 'override the first answer' test of our agent.

source: Evans, Barston, Pollard (1983) On the conflict between logic and belief in syllogistic reasoning (Mem Cognition)
finding: Not opened. From memory: belief bias; people accept believable conclusions more often regardless of logic, and the effect is larger for invalid ones. Recalled acceptance rates about 89 / 71 / 56 / 10 percent for valid-believable, invalid-believable, valid-unbelievable, invalid-unbelievable.
numbers: Recalled and unverified figures.
limits: Unverified. Later signal-detection work (Dube, Rotello and Heit 2010) argued the pattern may partly reflect response-bias artefacts; not checked here.
agent_relevance: Prior-belief pull on logic is a System 1 cue; strip belief cues before validity checks.

source: Neufeld et al. as reported in Pelaccia (2011)
finding: Early hypothesis effect: if the right diagnosis is among the first hypotheses (first five minutes), the final diagnosis is very likely right; if not, equally likely wrong. Dual-process reads early framing as intuition generating the candidate set.
numbers: About 95% chance of a correct final diagnosis when the correct hypothesis is considered in the first five minutes (secondhand).
limits: Secondhand figure; original study not opened; design and sample unknown.
agent_relevance: Candidate-set quality at the fast step bounds final accuracy: the slow step can only verify what the fast step offers. Argues for wide, diverse candidate generation at S0.
